courses.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: Consumer Product Design

evidence.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
evidence.profile: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
evidence.discipline: Product design; Product and process development; Sustainable design
evidence.topics: Consumer needs; Product concepts and specifications; Product working mechanisms; Prototyping; Laboratory-to-industrial production scaling; Materials and resource use; Product lifespan, repairability and circularity; Environmental impact; Production costs and commercial viability
evidence.methods: Consumer interviews; Needs ranking and specification development; Concept-criteria matrices; Quantitative product modelling; Product investigation and experimentation; Prototyping; Process-flow diagrams and material balances; Environmental-impact estimation; Break-even analysis

courses.name: Decision-making in AI

evidence.description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
evidence.profile: Develops the mathematical foundations of intelligent-agent decisions under uncertainty. Probability and Bayesian networks support belief updating and inference, while temporal models address changing environments. Decision theory, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems connect uncertainty to policies and expected utility. Multi-agent decisions introduce strategic and collective interaction, and probabilistic programming provides a framework for expressing models. Students work through equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

evidence.methods: Probabilistic inference; Bayesian-network modelling; Temporal probabilistic modelling; Expected-utility analysis; Sequential decision modelling; Game-theoretic analysis; Probabilistic programming

evidence.description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. judgment: The strongest positive composition has substantive mathematics, signals/control representations, consumer-product design, robot kinematics and renewable-energy engineering. Energy & Sustainability was added for actual physical resource/yield calculations, Polysun modelling, experiments and mini-grid design. Grant the official broader engineering/control description of Linear Systems and physical/material foundations of Sustainability Essentials I/II. Even with these contributions, the organising inquiry remains autonomous computation and energy/resource assessment. It does not sustain analysis of physical force, deformation, mechanical dynamics, thermal-fluid transport and material/manufacturing choices integrated through repeated mechanical-system design and testing. This is a programme-level material-response judgment, not equivalence, title/licence absence or a course-count quota. The environmental/resource candidate is coherent but moves further into geoscience, chemistry and sustainability rather than repairing this physical-engineering inquiry. A delta partner project does not guarantee a mechanical brief/supervision. No bounded supported substitution found in the current151-course catalogue supplies the missing spine.
